This is literally not true at all. You sign a bilateral contract with another party obligating you to purchase the home so long as all terms are executed by the parties. If you fail to carry through with your obligated terms, you can possibly be found in breach or default of contract and can open yourself up to a slew of legal repercussions, not the least of which is "specific performance". Although there are "exit ramps" out of most real estate contracts (such as not being able to agree on objections to condition of property), the notion that a Buyer can simply "walk away" in the middle of the contract is dangerously flawed.

Can you build in clauses that give the Buyer an easy “exit”? You bet. Will that Seller simply sign off on it? You never know, but in my experience, the answer is a hard no. Yikes...a lot of bad info in this thread.

1) Location, Location, Location. It may be cliche, but it's true. It's better to have the shittiest house in a nice neighborhood than a great house in a shitty neighborhood.

2) Get your head right. Most first time home-buyers don't have their heads right when going through this process the first time. You're not just buying a "house". You're making what is likely to be the most expensive and legally perilous purchase of your life. You need to consider the "investment" portion of your decision carefully. Understand the economic principles of progression and regression as it pertains to your real estate investment. Also (assuming you're in America), understand that when you buy property, you're not just buying the "house and the land", you're also buying a bundle of legal rights that come along with owning property. You need to inspect and understand these rights and ensure their security with just as much caution as you do your physical home inspection.

3) Contrary to some advice in here, do not buy a manufactured home. Manufactured homes are not built to the UBC and therefore depreciate (lose value) like personal property instead of gaining value like traditional real estate typically does (if you make a smart purchase). You can go the modular home route, which is kinda similar to manufactured, but is built to the UBC and therefore appreciates like real property.

4) Discover if you're in a "non-disclosure" state or not. If you're in a non-disclosure state, then ignore the online websites, as their data is likely to be inaccurate as they don't have access to proper market data.

5) Use real caution when putting together your team. Call around to some local title agencies and lenders. Ask who they recommend. Ask which Realtors put their clients first and their paychecks second. Ask which Realtors run the cleanest or tightest contracts. Ask which Realtors are advocates for their clients, and not themselves or their fellow Realtors. Don't just pick a Realtor based on their production. A lot of Realtors achieve high production by railroading first time home-buyers.

6) I typically recommend avoiding new construction for first time home-buyers. First time homebuyers don't typically stay in their first home for long. If you buy in new construction, and a few years later want to sell and move into a new neighborhood, you may still be competing with brand new houses as your development continues to be built. This is bad, as you'll have to cut your own throat to compete with the builders and all their perks. Additionally people looking in your neighborhood are going to be looking for a home that's never been lived in to "call their own".

7) Your lender will tell you how much you qualify for, not how much you can afford. These are often two VERY different values. Sit down, create a budget, and for fucks sake, live within your means. Just because you can qualify for a $300k house doesn't mean you can afford one.

8) Avoid the big 5 - Structural, Roof, Plumbing, Electrical, HVAC. If you find a home with any of these issues and the seller is either unable or unwilling to address them, then generally speaking, I'd advise you to walk. This is for two reasons. The first, when you go to sell, you'll need to take care of these issues or have big problems with marketability. These issues have a big impact on value, can be dangerous, and can be very expensive to address. The second reason to walk, if you have to take care of these issues, you get almost zero ROI (Return on Investment). If you put a new $8000 roof on your new house, it doesn't increase the value of your house by $8000. In fact, generally speaking, it doesn't increase the value of your home at all. That's the same for all of the big 5. Windows also fall under this category. Typically speaking, everything outside of the big 5 is cosmetic, and should bring some approximation of ROI, but with the big 5, although a great thing to do for a home, its not considered home improvement, it's considered maintenance.

9) Be careful with the mortgage you choose and don't sign shit until you truly understand what you're signing. There is a lot of predatory lending back out there, and these loan products are written to fuck you seven ways from Sunday. It's better to feel stupid asking stupid questions than it is to get foreclosed on. Even if they have to go through it a thousand times with you, DO NOT GET A MORTGAGE UNTIL YOU UNDERSTAND THE FINE PRINT.

...ok, I'm rambling a bit, I could go on about this stuff forever. Good luck OP

I've bought 4 now. Easily the #1 thing I wished I'd known up front was that a 30 year fixed mortgage isn't the best deal. Took till the 4th lender (having used small banks, big banks and dedicated mortgage broker) before anyone even Mentioned there might be better options. I'm on a 10:1 ARM (interest adjusts after 10 years, full pay-off at 15), it has the same Monthly cost as a 30yr/fixed but I will pay roughly 1/3rd the total interest.

People get scared by the "interest can adjust", but any lender worth their salt will be able to show you the EXACT change based on worst-case changes (interest can only adjust up a fixed/set amount). Easy enough for anyone with a couple brain cells to make a comparison. Bottom line for me is that I'm saving the same sum as the initial cost of my house.

Next to that is the old standard, location, location, location.... be Hyper aware. Are you within a block of something noisy (busy road, any kind of business, etc...), that WILL be noisy at all times of the day any night. Beyond that, you will sell the house at some point, so buying what sells well in a desirable location will mean a larger pool of shoppers and a faster sale... same vein, a house that has "issues" (cracks in foundation, "safety" things people freak out over) will shrink the pool and lower the value, as will bad schools/lack of amenities. Now, granted, YOU will also get that discounted price for those negatives, but I've made the mistake of being smart enough to know something wasn't an issue (functional/safety) only to run into shoppers who thought it Was an issue/unacceptable.

I like "needs work" places, but bit off more than I could chew the first time. I also like older homes (I've owned 2 from 1970's, one from 1950 and my current was built in 1930), the 1950 was easily the sweet spot for build and features... like having insulation. My 1930 is stunning, but it's expensive to live in daily (no insulation, everything is custom, takes much higher skill to maintain the whole house). You couldn't pay me to live in a New new house.

Rural Living - make damn sure the basement is dry, the septic works as it should and the well water is filtered. House I bought less than a year ago had none of those (I knew it buying the house and planned for it), if you don't have much experience with that stuff it can get expensive.

I wish I had been taught how to inspect it myself. There are so many things to watch out for. If the gutters are dirty or there aren't any, check, if possible, for any sort of water intrusion in the basement. Included in this is what is the landscaping like around the house. Does the ground slope away so that water doesn't collect at the foundation? Some people will let water pool near the foundation and that is bad. Keep an eye out for water damage of any kind. Bring someone with that has a great sense of smell to help detect mold or mildew odors. If they have one or more dehumidifiers in the basement its a sign that moisture might be an issue in that house. Consider the age of the house, and i would not recommend buying anything older than 40 years. Standards change, and you might find yourself having to replace something from an old standard and it makes repairs much harder. If the house has 2-prong electrical outlets these can be a bitch to replace with 3-prong. Inspect the water pipes in the house, if they are anything but copper or pex do not buy that house (mostly a problem in old houses). See if you can schedule a sewer pipe inspection. So many houses these days have huge looming issues with sewer pipes and the repairs are VERY expensive. The city I live in mandated sewer inspections and 75% of houses failed. Make sure the house has a good poop shoot. Keep an eye out for walls that sag, bow, or have cracks in them. Foundation cracks can be just fine depending on the pattern made by them. Do NOT fall for any sense of urgency expressed by any agent of any kind. This is a tactic they try on me constantly, but it helps if you don't HAVE to move, otherwise it can be very difficult to not feel the urgency. Find out how old the furnace or boiler is. Furnaces and boilers are very expensive items to replace, and furnaces that are 15 years or older are starting to get to "that age". If the house as an outside AC unit, find out how old that is. Standards in that area have changed a ton in the last 20 years, and upgrading or replacing an AC unit COULD require you to replace the coil at the furnace, or, worst case, to replace the AC unit may require replacing the furnace too. Find out what the property taxes are each year, you don't have to move very far to go from $2000/year to $7000/year in property taxes. I also wish i had paid more attention to proximity to convenience items such as hardware and grocery stores, as well as parks and walking/biking paths. Being close to a nice park will work wonders in being happy with location. I could go on forever, but one last item, do a quick visual of the neighbors houses. If the neighbors neglect their houses this will drag down the value of your house, and may indicate what kind of people they are. People with trashy yards, in my experience, are not good neighbors. On the flip side, if they neighbors houses are insanely manicured, they might be assholes to you if you don't do the same! Good luck! The housing market is insane right now.
